description: ODC (EDIT coverage over a STATIC ENTITY): maintain a static entity that THIS job did not create. The base is job:static-entity, so WfClaimStage, its four attributes, its three records and the WfClaimFile that consumes it already exist when the first op runs - there is not a single op that creates the model here, on purpose: creating and editing in the same job proves no maintenance at all. The changes are all made on top of what the other job left written: add the record WfEscalated to an entity that already had its three, rename two inherited records, rewrite the Label value of a record that already existed and rename the entity itself to WfClaimPhase. Outside the job that created them there are no aliases: the entity is cited as 'IStaticEntity:WfClaimStage', a record by the path 'IStaticEntity:WfClaimStage/Received' and the value of a column in that record as 'IStaticEntity:WfClaimStage/Received/Label' - three levels, resolved segment by segment, and the same form works inside args. TWO THINGS THAT ONLY AN EDIT JOB DISCOVERS, and which this job exists to pin down: (A) the record of a static entity is NOT renamed with the rename op in the ODC lane. The rename looks for the Name property in the Model API interfaces and the ODC IStaticEntityRecord has none - it publishes the record name as 'Identifier', whose getter returns Name and whose setter calls SetName, the same SetName as the Studio interface. The native path is therefore a set of Identifier, and propagation runs just the same. The entity, on the other hand, has Name and is renamed with the rename op: the job does both side by side. (B) renaming a record REWRITES the value of that record's Label column, but ONLY if that value is exactly the quotes around the old name (OnBeforeNameChange compares the text with "<OldName>" and only then swaps it). The job proves both branches: Received had Label "Received" and becomes "Intake" on its own; UnderReview had Label "Under review", which was never equal to the name, and stays intact when the record is renamed to Assessment - and only then is it set by hand to "Under assessment". THE CENTRAL PROOF remains the expression that cites Entities.<Entity>.<Record>: the inherited default of WfClaimFile.StageId said Entities.WfClaimStage.Received and this job never touches it before the renames - it is the platform that rewrites it on its own, first to Entities.WfClaimStage.Intake and then to Entities.WfClaimPhase.Intake. What does NOT follow along is read back next to it: the entity Description still cites WfClaimStage.Received word for word and the attribute name StageId still says Stage. At the end the inherited default is re-pointed to the NEW record, which closes the cycle: a record added today can be cited as Entities.<X>.<Y> like any of the inherited ones, and usages shows the consumer leaving Intake and entering WfEscalated. Wf prefix only on what is born here (WfEscalated): renaming something inherited follows the convention of whoever created it - Received/UnderReview/Closed carry no prefix, so Intake and Assessment do not either.

ops.name: WfClaimStage
ops._why: (0) the starting point is INHERITED: the static entity and the 'WfClaimStage Record' (the anonymous structure the platform generated with it) already exist before the first op of this job. They come from job:static-entity. Keep this list: the find (12g) makes it again after the entity rename and none of these names survives.

(1) BEFORE, the entity: EntityKind Static, Attributes 4, Records 3, Identifier/Label/OrderBy pointing to Id/Label/Order, and the Description that the other job wrote. Note the LabelAttribute: it is the column that branch (B) of the propagation will watch. Compare with the get (12c).

(2) BEFORE, the tree: 4 IEntityAttribute, 3 IStaticEntityRecord (Received, UnderReview, Closed), each with one IRecordAttributeValue per attribute and the value stored in an ITextBasedExpression, plus the GetWfClaimStage and the identifier generated by the platform. This is the snapshot the dump (14) is compared with.

(3) BEFORE, the ONLY real consumer of a record, also inherited: DataType 'WfClaimStage Identifier' and DefaultValue 'Entities.WfClaimStage.Received'. This text is not written by any op of this job - which is exactly why it works as proof: everything that happens to it from here on was done by the platform.

(4) BEFORE, who holds the Received record: count 1, real 1, and the consumer is the ITextBasedExpression of the WfClaimFile.StageId default. In ODC the expression property goes through ExpressionDefinition.Parse and is linked to the IStaticEntityRecord by KEY, not by text - and it is this link that makes the rest of the job work.
(5) BEFORE, who holds the ENTITY: the same default plus the IAttribute of the 'WfClaimStage Record'. It serves as a baseline for the usages (12f), after the entity changes its name.

(6) BEFORE, the value that will decide branch (A) of the propagation: an IRecordAttributeValue with Attribute = Label and Value = "Received" - exactly the record name between quotes. Keep the ObjectKey of this wrapper: the get (11e) reads the same one, with different text inside.

(7) BEFORE, the value that will decide branch (B): Value = "Under review", with a space, written by the other job. It is NOT equal to the record name (UnderReview), and this single difference of one space is what will separate the get (9d) from the get (11e). I chose a value ALREADY WRITTEN by an author and not an empty field, because only then is there a real replacement and not a fill-in.

ops.name: WfEscalated
ops._why: (8a) CHANGE 1 - add a record to an INHERITED static entity. The parent is not a $alias: aliases are local to the job that declares them and the one that declared this entity was another job; outside it the stable reference is 'IStaticEntity:WfClaimStage'. The type of the create is IRecord in both lanes, but the object that is born in ODC is an IStaticEntityRecord, and it already comes with an EMPTY IRecordAttributeValue for each of the four inherited attributes - the entity was not touched and yet the new record knows its columns. It carries the Wf prefix because it is born here; the inherited ones do not.
a static entity never has an Id AutoNumber: the new record receives its Id, the one after those of job:static-entity (Received 1, UnderReview 2, Closed 3).

the Value is an expression, so the text carries the OutSystems quotes inside the JSON quotes. $esc/<Attribute> reaches the value of that column in this record. Note that I write "Escalated" and not "WfEscalated": the record is already outside the rule of branch (B) from the start, and a future rename of it would not touch this label.
after the three inherited ones (1, 2, 3): the entity's OrderByAttribute is what governs the reading order, and the new record has to enter that sequence by hand - nothing does it for it.

escalating does not close the claim. It is the attribute BEYOND the trio Id/Label/Order, and it is what makes a new record cost four writes instead of one: each column of the static entity is one value per record.

(8b) AFTER: the new record. Note that the name comes out in the Identifier property and that there is NO Name - it is the first time this job shows it, and it is the fact that decides the form of ops (9b) and (11b). The alias $esc only exists because THIS job created it; it is the difference between what is inherited and what is added, and the reason all the other targets are paths.
the per-record value of the attribute that is not a label: IRecordAttributeValue with Attribute = IsFinal and Value = False.
(8c) the inherited entity seen again: Records went from 3 to 4 and Attributes is still 4. Adding a record does not touch the schema; compare with the get (1).

(8d) real 0: a record is born WITHOUT consumers, even inside an entity that already has one. It is not a defect, it is the meaning of the operation - and it is the reading that the usages (13d) will contradict at the end, after someone cites it.

(9a) BEFORE change 2: an INHERITED record read closely. Identifier = UnderReview, Referrers 0, and - once again - no Name property. Keep the ObjectKey: the get (9c) must bring the same one, otherwise what followed was a recreation and not an edit.

(9b) CHANGE 2, first half - rename an inherited record by the NATIVE path. In ODC, IStaticEntityRecord.Identifier reads and writes the record name: the getter returns Name and the setter calls SetName, the same SetName that the Studio interface calls when the name is edited in the records grid. There is no shortcut here - the rename op writes this same property (tests/jobs-odc/rename-name-property.json; until 2026-10-03 it looked for a Name that this type does not publish and refused with 'IStaticEntityRecord UnderReview has no Name'). Real difference compared to the rename op: the rename REFUSES a name collision, while this SetName calls AbstractObject.NameClash and adds a suffix SILENTLY, as the interface would - whoever writes has to make sure the name is free in the scope.

(9c) AFTER: Identifier = Assessment and the SAME ObjectKey as the get (9a) - no record was born, the name of one that already existed changed. The resolution path is also /Assessment now, because whoever resolves a child by name reads the same place that Identifier writes.

(9d) THE BRANCH WITHOUT PROPAGATION, proven: the Value is still "Under review". The record's OnBeforeNameChange looks for the value of the LabelAttribute column and only swaps it if it is exactly "<OldName>"; here it was "Under review" and the name was UnderReview, so there was no swap. Compare with the get (11e), where the same operation on the same type of object does the opposite - and the difference is one space in the text.

(9e) CHANGE 2, second half - the VALUE of an attribute in a record that ALREADY EXISTED, and at the same time the manual fix for what (9d) showed does not follow along. It is not the record name nor the Label property of an object: it is the content of the Label column IN THIS record, the text the user reads in a dropdown. Three-level target: entity, record, attribute.

(9f) AFTER: compare with the get (7) and (9d). The Value CHANGED; the Attribute pointing to the same Label column and the same IRecordAttributeValue ObjectKey STAYED - the value was rewritten in place, there was no new wrapper.
(9g) real 0, before and after: this inherited record never had consumers. It serves as counter-proof to the usages (11f) - what changes from record to record is not the operation, it is who cites it.

ops.value: Etapas de um sinistro. O valor por omissao de WfClaimFile.StageId e Entities.WfClaimStage.Received.
ops._why: (10) THE TRAP, SET ON PURPOSE, BEFORE the renames still to come: author text that cites an entity and a record by name. From op (11b) on, both citations become wrong and nothing corrects them - the get (12c) reads them back word for word. It is the exact counterpoint of the expression: the Description and the DefaultValue say the same thing, and only the second is model.

(11a) BEFORE change 3: the other inherited record, and the difference that matters is in Referrers = 1 - this one has a consumer, the one in the get (9a) had none. Identifier = Received, and the ObjectKey is the one that the get (11c) must repeat.

(11b) CHANGE 3 - the second record rename, now on a record WITH a real consumer and with the Label equal to the name. Same verb as (9b), same entity, another record: that is what makes the comparison honest.
(11c) AFTER: Identifier = Intake, the same ObjectKey as the get (11a), and Referrers still 1 - the consumer did not come loose.

(11d) THE CENTRAL PROOF: the inherited DefaultValue already says Entities.WfClaimStage.Intake, without a single manual fix. Compare with the get (3). Nobody wrote this text: the expression was linked to the record by key and the platform regenerated it when the SetName ran. It is also the proof that writing Identifier is not a label shortcut - if it were, this expression would have stayed saying Received and the module would fail at Verify.

(11e) THE BRANCH WITH PROPAGATION, proven: the same wrapper as the get (6), the same ObjectKey, and the Value went from "Received" to "Intake" ON ITS OWN, with no op writing it. It is the OnBeforeNameChange: the value of the Label column was exactly "Received", the quotes around the old name, and so the platform swapped it. Put this get next to (9d) - two sibling records, the same operation, opposite results, and the whole rule fits in the comparison of one string. Anyone who had only renamed THIS record would leave here believing the Label always follows along; anyone who had only renamed the other would leave believing it never follows.

(11f) the same list as the usages (4), with the same consumer key and the text already rewritten: changing the name did not touch whoever uses it. Note that here there is no consumers counter or expressionsRewritten to consult - the set does not return them -, and that is exactly why this job reads everything with get and usages: the AGENTS.md already warns that the counter changes meaning with the object type and that the proof is in the reading.

ops.name: Received
ops._why: (11g) the record of this entity no longer answers to Received, which settles the doubt about whether Identifier was a second field next to the name; what the list brings is the signature of a namesake elsewhere in the module, not this record. The text "Received" is also no longer in this record's Label - the branch with propagation took it.

ops.name: WfClaimPhase
ops._why: (12a) CHANGE 4 - rename the inherited entity ITSELF, with a real consumer linked and two records already renamed inside. Here the rename op WORKS, because IEntitySignature publishes a writable Name: it is the direct contrast with (9b) and (11b), and the reason this job uses two different verbs for the same intent. It returns consumers=2 and expressionsRewritten=1 - the expression counted is the default; the other consumer is the IAttribute of the 'WfClaimStage Record', which follows by key and has no text to rewrite. It keeps the Wf prefix because it inherited it from the old name, not because it is born here.

(12b) THE CENTRAL PROOF, second half: the DefaultValue now says Entities.WfClaimPhase.Intake - BOTH parts of the citation were rewritten, each by its own rename and by different verbs, and neither by this job. It is the same inherited attribute as in the get (3) and the get (11d). The DataType also followed, because the identifier type is generated by the entity and is not text. What did NOT follow is in the same get: the attribute is still named StageId and its Label still says 'Stage'.

(12c) AFTER, the entity: compare with the get (1). The Name, the ReadableIdentifier and the derived Label/LabelPlural ('Wf Claim Phase') CHANGED, and Records is 4; the ObjectKey, the EntityKind Static, the Identifier/Label/OrderBy pointing to the same attributes STAYED and - the point - so did the Description of op (10), which still says WfClaimStage.Received, two names that no longer exist in this entity. Description is author text: no rename touches it, and neither of the two verbs used in this job makes any difference to that.

(12d) WHAT STAYED: an inherited attribute that this job did not touch - Boolean, with the Description that the other job wrote. Side by side with the get (9f) it shows that the edit went TO the chosen records and not to the whole entity.

(12e) WHAT STAYED: the consuming entity, intact - the same Description, the same 3 attributes, the same index, the same entity actions. Renaming the static entity does not rebuild whoever uses it; only the text of the expressions inside it was regenerated.

(12f) compare with the usages (5): the SAME two consumer keys, with the new names in the texts. The consumers stay linked by key, and that is why the rename can rewrite the text without losing anyone.

ops.name: WfClaimStage
ops._why: (12g) EMPTY list: compare with the find (0). The entity and the 'WfClaimStage Record' disappeared together, because the second is generated FROM the entity and is not author text.

ops.name: WfClaimPhase
ops._why: (12h) and this is where they reappear, with the new name, without a single op asking for it. This pair of finds is the cheap proof that renaming an entity is more than swapping a label.

(13a) THE CYCLE CLOSES: the inherited default, which this job read four times without touching, is now RE-POINTED by hand to the record created in op (8a). Proof that a record added today can be cited as Entities.<X>.<Y> exactly like the inherited ones, and that the citation must already use the two new names - written with WfClaimStage.Received, the Parse would find nothing. It is the only op in the job that writes an expression, and it comes AFTER the renames on purpose: written before, the platform would rewrite it and what was read back would no longer be what the job asked for - the data contract compares the requested text with the text read and would fail the delivery.
(13b) AFTER: the text is what this job wrote, not what the platform regenerated. Fifth read of the same inherited attribute, and the first in which the change is the author's.

(13c) the renamed record is left WITHOUT real consumers: what held it was this default, and it changed target. Compare with the usages (4) and (11f) - three reads of the same record, with the same format, and only the third changes.

(13d) and the consumer is now on the new record: real 1, against the real 0 of the usages (8d). It is the pair that shows that a static entity record is a model object like any other - with consumers, with delete refusal and with usages that are read before and after.

(14) the final tree, to put next to the dump (2): the 4 inherited attributes in the same order and with the same keys, 4 IStaticEntityRecord instead of 3 with WfEscalated at the END of the sequence, the record that was Received now Intake and with the Label that the PLATFORM rewrote for it, the one that was UnderReview now Assessment and with the Label that an AUTHOR had to rewrite, and the entity action and the identifier with the new name. What the platform redid is all here; what was left for the author is too - and that is the Description, which still points to two dead names.
